title: Σῦς ⟨ἄγριος⟩ καὶ ἵππος καὶ κυνηγέτης
titleEn: The Wild Boar, the Horse and the Hunter
part: The Wild Boar, the Horse and the Hunter (Chambry 328 · Perry 269)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 328 (= Perry 269). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements, [ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Σῦς ἄγριος καὶ ἵππος ἐν ταὐτῷ ἐνέμοντο.
sentences.tr: Sys agrios kai hippos en tautōi enemonto.
sentences.l: A wild boar and a horse were grazing in the same place.
sentences.n: ταὐτῷ is τῷ αὐτῷ run together by crasis, 'the same'. νέμομαι in the middle is what the beasts do for themselves — graze, feed on the pasture; in the active the same verb is what the herdsman does to them.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ συὸς παρ’ ἕκαστα τὴν πόαν διαφθείροντος καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ θολοῦντος, ὁ ἵππος βουλόμενος αὐτὸν ἀμύνασθαι [ἐπὶ] κυνηγέτην σύμμαχον παρέλαβε.
sentences.tr: Tou de syos par’ hekasta tēn poan diaphtheirontos kai to hydōr tholountos, ho hippos boulomenos auton amynasthai [epi] kynēgetēn symmachon parelabe.
sentences.l: And the boar at every turn spoiling the grass and muddying the water, the horse, wishing to take revenge on him, took a hunter as ally.
sentences.i: Since the boar was forever ruining the grass and fouling the water, the horse, wanting to pay him out, took a hunter as his ally.
sentences.n: A genitive absolute again (τοῦ … συός … διαφθείροντος … θολοῦντος), the fable's regular way of setting up the grievance. παρ’ ἕκαστα is 'at every turn, on each occasion'. ἀμύνομαι in the middle is to fend a man off from oneself, and so to requite him. Chambry brackets [ἐπί] as interpolated: παραλαμβάνω wants κυνηγέτην as its plain object, and a preposition standing in front of it would leave the verb without one. Nothing in the English answers to the bracketed word.

sentences.t: Κἀκείνου εἰπόντος μὴ ἄλλως δύνασθαι αὐτῷ βοηθεῖν, ἐὰν μὴ χαλινόν τε ὑπομείνῃ καὶ αὐτὸν ἐπιβάτην δέξηται, ὁ ἵππος πάντα ὑπέστη.
sentences.tr: Kakeinou eipontos mē allōs dynasthai autōi boēthein, ean mē chalinon te hypomeinēi kai auton epibatēn dexētai, ho hippos panta hypestē.
sentences.l: And he having said that he could help him in no other way, unless he should submit to a bridle and receive him as rider, the horse undertook it all.
sentences.i: And when the man said he could help him in no other way unless the horse would submit to a bridle and take him on his back as rider, the horse agreed to everything.
sentences.n: ὑπομένω is to stand firm under a thing, to submit to it. ὑφίσταμαι (aorist ὑπέστη) is to take a thing upon oneself, to undertake it — and both verbs carry the ὑπο- of going underneath, which is exactly where the horse is about to find himself.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ κυνηγέτης ἐποχηθεὶς αὐτῷ καὶ τὸν σῦν κατηγωνίσατο καὶ τὸν ἵππον προσαγαγὼν τῇ φάτνῃ προσέδησεν.
sentences.tr: Kai ho kynēgetēs epochētheis autōi kai ton syn katēgōnisato kai ton hippon prosagagōn tēi phatnēi prosedēsen.
sentences.l: And the hunter, having ridden upon him, both overcame the boar and, having led the horse up to the manger, tied him fast to it.
sentences.i: And the hunter, mounted on him, overcame the boar, and then led the horse to the manger and tied him fast there.
sentences.n: καὶ … καί is 'both … and', and the pairing is the sting: one and the same ride wins the boar's defeat and the horse's halter. ἐποχηθείς is an aorist passive of ἐποχέομαι used in the middle sense, 'having mounted'.

sentences.t: Οὕτω πολλοὶ δι’ ἀλόγιστον ὀργήν, ἕως τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ἀμύνασθαι θέλουσιν, ἑαυτοὺς ἑτέροις ὑπορρίπτουσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtō polloi di’ alogiston orgēn, heōs tous echthrous amynasthai thelousin, heautous heterois hyporriptousin.
sentences.l: Thus many, through unreasoning anger, so long as they wish to requite their enemies, throw themselves down under others.
sentences.n: ἕως with the indicative is 'so long as, all the while that'. ὑπορρίπτω is to throw a thing down beneath another; used of oneself it is to make oneself another man's creature — the horse under the saddle, and then under the halter.
